hero.safeText: Only from official repositories. Installers are verified by checksum and go through antivirus checks.

safe.lead: HubGet installs only apps from verified sources and checks every installer before running it.

sources.title: Official repositories
sources.text: Apps come from Microsoft’s WinGet, Chocolatey and Scoop. HubGet doesn’t repackage or modify them.

checksum.title: SHA-256 checksum
checksum.text: The downloaded installer is compared with the fingerprint from the repository. If someone tampered with it on the way, the installation won’t start.

antivirus.title: Virus checks
antivirus.text: Packages in WinGet and Chocolatey go through automated virus scanning when they’re approved, and the antivirus in Windows checks the installer when it runs.

publishers.title: Verified publishers
publishers.text: A blue check next to the name means an official publisher – Microsoft, Mozilla, VideoLAN and others – from an official repository.

simple.lead: Installs without setup wizards, without clicking Next and without offers you don’t want.

silent.title: Silent install
silent.text: The installer runs in the background with default settings and no questions, and HubGet lets you know when it’s done. Turn the wizard on in install options.

noExtras.title: No add-ons or ads
noExtras.text: Screens offering bundled software don’t appear during a silent install. HubGet has no ads.

queue.title: Several apps at once
queue.text: Pick several apps or a whole bundle – they install one after another in a queue with progress in percent, even after you close the window.

fallback.title: Fallback source
fallback.text: When a WinGet download link is broken, HubGet tries Chocolatey or Scoop on its own.

manage.lead: All the apps on your PC in one place – including those you installed earlier or some other way.

overview.title: Installed apps overview
overview.text: HubGet finds apps from WinGet, Chocolatey, Scoop, the Microsoft Store and games from Steam, and checks that they’re really on your PC.

updates.title: Updates
updates.text: See available updates in one place and install them all at once – or let HubGet install them on its own at a time you choose.

uninstall.title: Uninstall and clean up

help.title: Help
help.subtitle: Answers to common questions and where to turn when you're stuck

how.a: HubGet doesn't download or modify anything itself. It hands the installation to a package manager – WinGet, Chocolatey, Scoop, or for developer tools npm or pip, for example – and shows its progress. Packages come straight from the official repositories.

source.q: Where is an app installed from when it's in several sources?
source.a: From the first enabled source in the order you set in <settings>Settings</settings>. You can pick the source manually on the app's profile. An installed app is updated through the source it was installed from.

uac.q: Why does the User Account Control (UAC) window appear?
uac.a: Some installers write to system folders and therefore need administrator rights; Chocolatey always requires them. HubGet asks for permission only for that specific operation – it never runs entirely as administrator.

bundles.q: How do I install several apps at once?
bundles.a: Add them to a <bundles>package bundle</bundles> (the plus icon on an app's card). Then install the bundle in one click, save it to a file, or create a PowerShell script for another PC.

failed.a: The <history>operation history</history> shows what failed and lets you retry. Details are in the <logs>package manager logs</logs>. Trying another source or closing an app that blocks the installer often helps.

safe.q: Is installing through HubGet safe? Can I get a virus?
safe.a: Yes – it's the safest way to install apps. HubGet doesn't download programs from random websites with fake “Download” buttons, only from the package managers' official repositories. Microsoft checks WinGet packages (SmartScreen, static analysis) and WinGet verifies the installer's SHA-256 checksum before installing, so a tampered installer won't get through. Chocolatey packages go through moderation and VirusTotal antivirus scanning, and Scoop verifies the checksum from its manifest. Nothing is bundled with the installer and HubGet doesn't modify it. For developer libraries and tools (npm, PyPI, crates.io…) the author is responsible for the content – install them from publishers you trust. HubGet is open source and sends no personal data without signing in.

add.q: An app or source is missing. How do I add it?
add.a: Apps get into HubGet through the package managers' repositories – see the <publish>Publish</publish> page for how. You can suggest a new package source with the “Add source” button in the sidebar.

commands.title: Terminal commands
commands.subtitle: Everything HubGet does with a click, you can also do from the command line. Pick a package manager and copy a command.
commands.howTo: Run the commands in Windows Terminal or PowerShell. The examples use one sample app and can be copied as they are – you'll find the exact command for any other app on its page, in the “… from the command line” section.
commands.howToPlaceholders: Run the commands in Windows Terminal or PowerShell. Replace <package> (<ID> for WinGet) with the package and <name> with what you're looking for – you'll find the exact command for a specific app on its page, in the “… from the command line” section.

note.winget: WinGet comes with Windows 10 and 11 (App Installer). It looks apps up by their exact ID – find it on the app's page or with winget search.
note.chocolatey: Installing, updating and uninstalling with Chocolatey needs a Terminal run as administrator.
note.scoop: Scoop installs into your user folder without admin rights. Apps live in buckets – add “extras” (Firefox, VLC…) with scoop bucket add extras.
note.npm: Global npm packages are command-line tools (TypeScript, ESLint…). npm comes with Node.js.
note.bun: Bun is a fast replacement for Node.js and npm. It adds global packages with bun add -g; updating means installing again with @latest.
note.pip: pip installs Python packages. Run it as python -m pip – that uses the pip of the Python on your PATH. Searching PyPI from the command line isn't possible, use pypi.org.
note.cargo: Cargo is Rust's package manager – cargo install builds a tool from source. The install command also installs a newer version.
note.vcpkg: vcpkg manages C and C++ libraries (classic mode – no vcpkg.json in a project).
note.dotnet: .NET tools (dotnet tool) install globally into your user folder. They need the .NET SDK.
note.powershell: Windows PowerShell 5.1 modules via PowerShellGet (*-Module commands).

welcome.title: Welcome to HubGet
welcome.text: An app store for Windows. In a minute we'll show you what it can do.
welcome.point2: Safe, from official sources – no viruses, ads or bundled extras
welcome.point3: Install, update and uninstall in one click

catalog.title: One universal catalog
catalog.text: Apps from WinGet, Chocolatey and Scoop under one roof. Each app has one card with every source – HubGet picks the best one, or you choose.
catalog.point1: Search across all package managers at once
catalog.point2: If an install from one source fails, another is offered
catalog.point3: In Developer mode, npm, pip, Cargo and more too

reviews.title: Ratings and reviews
reviews.text: See how other users rate apps and read their reviews. Sign in with GitHub to add your own rating, review or current screenshots.
reviews.point1: The star average and the most helpful reviews in one place
reviews.point2: Edit or delete your own review any time, report inappropriate ones
reviews.point3: Signing in is optional – everything else works without an account

filter.title: Filter by source
filter.text: Only want apps from WinGet? Click the source in the sidebar – the catalog, search and installs are limited to it.

filter.point2: Click again or “Show all sources” to clear it
filter.point3: Works for developer package managers too

notifications.title: Notifications and updates
notifications.text: The result of every install, update and uninstall is under the bell at the top right – including what HubGet did in the background.
notifications.point1: Errors come with the full message – click to copy it
notifications.point2: An orange dot on the icon by the clock means updates are available
notifications.point3: The full operation history is one click away
notifications.where: Choose what gets announced in Settings → Notification preferences.

uninstall.title: Advanced uninstall
uninstall.text: After an uninstall, HubGet finds what the app left behind – folders, shortcuts and registry entries – and offers to clean them up, much like Revo Uninstaller.
uninstall.point1: Files go to the Recycle Bin, registry keys are backed up first
uninstall.point2: With install monitoring, it removes exactly what the installer created
uninstall.point3: Ends the app's running processes before uninstalling
uninstall.toggleHint: Searches Program Files, ProgramData and the registry besides AppData.

startup.title: Startup apps and backups
startup.text: Speed up Windows startup: see what starts when you sign in and turn off what you don't need. Move your app profile and settings to another PC.
startup.point1: The startup impact of each item
startup.point2: Profile export to JSON or a readable HTML page
startup.point3: Import installs missing apps in one click
startup.where: Find them in the sidebar (Startup apps) and in Settings → Backup and catalog.

settings.closeBackgroundProcesses: Close an app running in the background without asking
settings.closeBackgroundProcessesHint: Before an install, update or uninstall, HubGet ends the app's processes that have no window (such as a tray icon or a process stuck in memory). An app with an open window gets a one-click offer to close it.
settings.forceCloseRunningHint: Before an install, update or uninstall, HubGet closes the running app itself – like clicking its close button. If the app asks to save your work, HubGet waits until you save it and close the app; an app hidden in the notification area or one that isn't responding is force closed. Off: HubGet asks first. Automatic background updates don't close an app with an open window – they wait.
settings.advancedUninstall: Advanced uninstall with a leftover scan (registry and files)
settings.advancedUninstallHint: After an uninstall, it searches Program Files, ProgramData, Start menu and desktop shortcuts and the Windows registry (HKCU and HKLM\Software) besides AppData, and offers to delete the leftovers. Files go to the Recycle Bin; registry keys are backed up before they're deleted.

settings.autoCleanupHint: Leftovers are deleted right after the uninstall and you only get a short notification. Items in Program Files or HKLM need administrator rights – Windows asks once.
settings.newsCurrentHint: The window with new features shown after an update – in case you closed it by accident.

Whatever the installer created is saved with the app and offered for removal after an uninstall – even without advanced uninstall. Installs take a few seconds longer. You can monitor a single app without this setting too: right-click → Install with monitoring.

security.warning: The following settings may pose a security risk, so they are disabled by default. Enable them IF AND ONLY IF you fully understand what they do and what consequences and dangers they may have.
security.elevationTitle: Change how operations request administrator rights
security.elevateAlways: Ask for administrator rights for every operation
security.elevateAlwaysHint: Every install, update and uninstall via WinGet and Chocolatey runs with administrator rights (UAC prompt). Scoop always runs without them.
security.elevateOnce: Ask for administrator rights only once
security.elevateOnceHint: After the first UAC confirmation, the elevated HubGet helper keeps running until the app exits and further operations are elevated without asking. It only accepts installs by id from official sources – anything else still needs UAC.
security.elevationProhibited: Prohibit any elevation via HubGet Elevator or Gsudo
security.elevationProhibitedHint: This option will cause problems. Any operation that can't elevate itself will fail.
security.broker: Delegate package operations to the Devolutions Agent broker
security.brokerHint: In companies with privilege management (Devolutions PEDM) the agent would run operations instead of HubGet. HubGet doesn't support delegation yet – so the switch is off; the check below shows the agent's state.
security.brokerWeb: Available only in the desktop app.
security.brokerDirect: operations run directly in HubGet (no broker)
security.allowCustomArgsHint: Install options will accept custom installer arguments. Without this the backend ignores them (arguments from HubGet options – PATH, no restart – keep working).
security.allowPrePost: Allow running custom pre-install and post-install commands
security.allowPrePostHint: Install options will accept commands (cmd) that run before and after the install – with your rights.
security.allowPaths: Allow changing package manager executable paths
security.allowPathsHint: HubGet uses the given winget.exe, choco.exe or scoop.ps1 instead of the one found in the system.
security.importCustomArgs: Allow importing custom command-line arguments when importing packages from a bundle
security.importCustomArgsHint: Otherwise custom arguments from the bundle file (.ubundle) are dropped.
security.importPrePost: Allow importing custom pre-install and post-install commands when importing packages from a bundle
security.importPrePostHint: Otherwise commands from the bundle file are dropped – a bundle from someone else can't run anything.
security.noWaitHint: Updates whose release notes say they fix a security issue (CVE, “security fix”) are offered and installed right away – they don’t wait for the minimum age.
security.osvHint: For Developer mode packages (npm, Bun, pip, Cargo, .NET Tool), checks the installed versions against the open vulnerability database OSV.dev. Only the package name and version are sent.
